subtopicTitle: Quaternion rotation formula — rotating vector v by quaternion q

cards.front: How is a 3D vector \(\vec{v}=(x,y,z)\) represented as a quaternion for rotation purposes?
cards.back: As the pure quaternion \(v = 0 + xi + yj + zk\).

cards.front: State the quaternion rotation formula that rotates vector \(v\) by unit quaternion \(q\).
cards.back: $v' = q v q^{-1}$ (where \(v\) and \(v'\) are pure quaternions).

cards.front: For a unit quaternion \(q = w + xi + yj + zk\), what is \(q^{-1}\)?
cards.back: $q^{-1} = w - xi - yj - zk$ (i.e., the conjugate).

cards.front: After applying \(v' = q v q^{-1}\), what is the scalar (real) part of \(v'\)?
cards.back: Exactly zero, confirming \(v'\) remains a pure quaternion/vector.

cards.front: Why does the formula preserve vector length only when \(\|q\|=1\)?
Write the three-step quaternion multiplication sequence to obtain the rotated vector components.
cards.back: 1. Compute \(p = q v\) (4 multiplies). 2. Compute \(v' = p q^{-1}\). 3. Discard the resulting scalar part.

cards.front: A rotation quaternion is \(q = \cos(	heta/2) + \sin(	heta/2)\hat{u}\). What angle does \(v' = q v q^{-1}\) actually apply to \(\vec{v}\)?
Show that \(q=1\) and \(q=-1\) both produce the identity rotation.
cards.back: Both yield \(v' = v\), since \(1\cdot v\cdot 1^{-1}=v\) and \((-1)v(-1)^{-1}=v\).
